authors: Cortes, Jackel, Solla, Vapnik and Denker
title: Learning curves: asymptotic values and rate of convergence
why: Power-law learning curves fitted on small training sets to predict large-set error; the 1993 origin of the method. NIPS 6. Not on arXiv.

title: Scaling to very very large corpora for natural language disambiguation
why: Accuracy keeps rising log-linearly with corpus size across a billion words, and simple models catch up with complex ones. ACL 2001. Not on arXiv.

title: The unreasonable effectiveness of data
why: The essay that made 'more data beats cleverer algorithms' a slogan. IEEE Intelligent Systems 24(2). Not on arXiv.

title: Revisiting unreasonable effectiveness of data in deep learning era
why: JFT-300M: vision performance grows logarithmically with data over three orders of magnitude.

title: Deep learning scaling is predictable, empirically
why: Power-law generalization error across translation, speech, vision and language (character-LM exponent -0.094); the first modern 'scaling is predictable' paper.

title: AI and compute (OpenAI blog)
why: The 3.4-month doubling of training compute from 2012 to 2018. Secondary source; not on arXiv.

title: A constructive prediction of the generalization error across scales
why: A joint functional form in model size and data that predicts error across scales, before Kaplan.

title: Compute trends across three eras of machine learning
why: Epoch's reconstruction of training-compute growth; the context for every 'how much compute' number.

title: Scaling laws for neural language models
why: Power laws in N, D and C over seven orders of magnitude, the 6ND cost model, the critical batch size, and the first compute-optimal allocation.

title: Language models are few-shot learners
why: GPT-3: the first frontier model whose size was justified by Kaplan's law; Figure 3.1 is the law extended to 175B.

title: Scaling laws for autoregressive generative modeling
why: The same laws for images, video, math and multimodal models; the loss floor and the irreducible term.

title: Training compute-optimal large language models
why: Chinchilla: three methods, the parametric fit L = E + A/N^a + B/D^b, and the 20-tokens-per-parameter rule that replaced Kaplan's allocation.

title: Chinchilla scaling: a replication attempt
why: Re-fits Chinchilla's third method from the paper's own figure and finds different constants; a lesson in fitting.

title: Resolving discrepancies in compute-optimal scaling of language models
why: Why Kaplan and Chinchilla disagreed: embedding parameters, warmup, and learning-rate tuning at small scale.

title: An empirical model of large-batch training
why: The gradient-noise scale and the critical batch size; the source of Kaplan's B_crit law.

title: Beyond Chinchilla-optimal: accounting for inference in language model scaling laws
why: Add the inference cost 2N·D_inf to the objective: models that will be served a lot should be smaller and trained longer.

title: Language models scale reliably with over-training and on downstream tasks
why: Laws fitted at up to 32x over-training extrapolate reliably; also fits the loss-to-average-downstream-error curve used in Section 5.

title: Scaling data-constrained language models
why: Repeating data up to about four epochs is nearly free; the decay constants for repeated tokens and excess parameters.

title: Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data
why: Epoch's estimate of the public text stock and when training runs exhaust it (revised in 2024).

title: DeepSeek LLM: scaling open-source language models with longtermism
why: Hyperparameter scaling laws (learning rate and batch size against compute), the non-embedding FLOPs-per-token M, and a careful compute-optimal fit.

title: Tensor Programs V: tuning large neural networks via zero-shot hyperparameter transfer
why: muP: parameterize so that the optimal learning rate does not move with width, then tune on a small model.

title: MiniCPM: unveiling the potential of small language models with scalable training strategies
why: Warmup-stable-decay schedules and muP in a practical small-model ladder; the WSD trick that makes ladders cheap.

title: Scaling laws and compute-optimal training beyond fixed training durations
why: With a constant learning rate and short cooldowns, one run yields loss at many token counts; scaling experiments at a fraction of the cost.

title: Cerebras-GPT: open compute-optimal language models trained on the Cerebras wafer-scale cluster
why: A public Chinchilla-style ladder with muP, reporting the fits and the gain from muP in practice.

title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale transformer training instabilities
why: Instabilities that appear at scale (attention-logit growth, output-logit divergence) reproduced in small models by raising the learning rate; what to watch on a ladder.

title: Unified scaling laws for routed language models
why: The first scaling law with the number of experts as a variable.

title: Scaling laws for fine-grained mixture of experts
why: Granularity as a law variable; MoE beats dense at every scale when tuned.

title: Scaling laws with vocabulary: larger models deserve larger vocabularies
why: The compute-optimal vocabulary size grows with model size; most models' vocabularies are too small.

title: Scaling laws for precision
why: Precision as a third resource: effective parameters N(1 - e^{-P/gamma}), a 7-8 bit optimum, and the post-training quantization penalty.

title: Data mixing laws: optimizing data mixtures by predicting language modeling performance
why: Loss as a function of domain mixture proportions, fitted on small runs to choose the mix for a large one.

title: Emergent abilities of large language models
why: Benchmarks that jump from chance to competence at a scale threshold; the case that capability is not smooth in loss.

title: Are emergent abilities of large language models a mirage?
why: The jumps come from discontinuous metrics (exact match) on smoothly improving per-token accuracy.

title: GPT-4 technical report
why: Section 3: loss and a coding pass rate predicted from runs with 1,000-10,000x less compute.

title: The Llama 3 herd of models
why: Section 3.2.1: a two-stage law, compute to loss and loss to benchmark accuracy, used to set the 405B model's size.

title: Establishing task scaling laws via compute-efficient model ladders
why: A ladder of small models predicts task accuracy of 7B and 13B models within a few points; the ladder method made explicit.

title: Scaling laws for downstream task performance in machine translation
why: When downstream metrics follow the pretraining loss and when they do not (distribution mismatch).

title: Explaining neural scaling laws
why: Variance-limited and resolution-limited regimes; exponents tied to the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold.

title: Learning curve theory
why: A Zipf-distributed feature model that produces power-law learning curves from first principles.

title: The quantization model of neural scaling
why: Skills ('quanta') learned in order of frequency under a Zipf law give the observed exponents and the jumps underneath smooth loss.

title: A neural scaling law from the dimension of the data manifold
why: Exponent alpha ~ 4/d for data on a d-dimensional manifold; the geometric argument behind Bahri et al.

title: A hitchhiker's guide to scaling law estimation
why: A large-scale study of how to fit and extrapolate laws: which models, how many, intermediate checkpoints, and the usual errors.

title: 2 OLMo 2 furious
why: A fully open training run with ladders, stability fixes and mid-training; the practice companion to Bhagia et al.

title: Understanding warmup-stable-decay learning rates: a river valley loss landscape perspective
why: Why the WSD schedule works and why the decay phase gives the loss that ladders compare.

title: Scaling laws for transfer
why: Effective data transferred from pretraining to fine-tuning follows a power law; how much pretraining is worth in fine-tuning tokens.

title: Frontier pre-training at Microsoft AI (MAI-Base-2 report)
why: The case study of the deck's frontier section: ladders, hyperparameter transfer and the final run. Not on arXiv; the PDF was supplied for the lecture.

title: DeepSeek-V3 technical report
why: A frontier run whose report shows the ladder (16B and 230B MoE pilots) before the 671B model.
